content: These bursts were NMDAR and gap junction dependent. Wwox-knockout neocortical slices show spontaneous layer II/III bursting abolished by d-APV (D-AP5).

note: Sole WWOX-specific NMDAR datum; slice network activity. Report calls the preparation "young-mouse" at L33 (age not given). Source also reports (verifier, full text) a larger delayed evoked response in the knockout that d-APV reversibly suppresses (Supplementary Fig S3), a neuron-specific Synapsin-Cre model, bursts in heterozygotes (4 of 23 slices; 0 of 11 wild type), and an authors caveat that the age may mimic a late-stage disorder.

content: d-APV profile: competitive antagonist at GluN2 glutamate site; voltage-, Mg2+- and use-independent; pan-GluN2 (all GluN1/GluN2 diheteromers); blocks tonic drive; poor BBB penetration; no clinical status; competitive block surmountable by glutamate (L18).
anchor: L9,L16-L25,L30,L55-L65 Summary; Reference Pharmacology; Mechanistic model
note: Properties asserted without a per-property citation; table and ASCII diagram repeat them.

content: Because d-APV blocks all NMDAR current whatever the channel state, its abolition of the burst does not reveal which GluN2 subunit carries the burst or whether the drive is tonic or phasic.
anchor: L26,L67 Reference Pharmacology; Why the transfer is not automatic
note: Framing of the two key unknowns.

content: Gap-junction co-dependence does not undermine NMDAR targeting: d-APV alone abolishes the burst, so NMDAR block is sufficient and a drug need only hit the NMDAR arm.
note: Tension with E05 (same report, L132).

content: NMDAR block and gap-junction block may act in series or in parallel; an NMDA antagonist that reduces but does not abolish the burst could reflect electrical coupling sustaining residual activity.
note: Qualifies E04; also motivates combination arm E69.

content: No approved drug shares d-APV's profile; clinical NMDA antagonists are either uncompetitive open-channel pore blockers or GluN2B-selective allosteric modulators.
note: Class assignment of each named drug is uncited except memantine.

content: Memantine: uncompetitive, low-affinity open-channel blocker that "enters the receptor-associated ion channel preferentially when it is excessively open"; off-rate relatively fast.
note: Quote at L30 is 11 words; second quote at L45 is longer than 25 words so paraphrased here.

content: Ketamine: open-channel pore blocker; CNS-penetrant; used in refractory/super-refractory status epilepticus; proposed potent positive control and acute rescue, not chronic therapy.

note: Carries highest developmental-neurotoxicity burden per report.

content: Amantadine named as a use-/voltage-dependent pore blocker (weak open-channel); lower priority; matrix: CNS exposure Good (+), approved (L93).
note: Matrix gives developmental safety "Uncertain".

content: Dextromethorphan/dextrorphan named as pore blocker; matrix flags CYP2D6-limited exposure (with quinidine), developmental concern; "weak, discouraging encephalopathy data"; lower priority.

content: Nitrous oxide named as channel blocker (inhaled, approved, neurotoxic in matrix); lower priority.
note: Neurotoxicity asserted without citation.

content: Radiprodil: GluN2B-selective negative allosteric modulator (ATD site); inhibits GluN2B NMDARs "with high potency and selectivity and appears to be safe in humans".
note: Lead candidate. Report asserts it is voltage- and use-independent like d-APV (E14) without a citation.

content: Radiprodil is an effective antagonist at the majority of disease-associated GRIN1/GRIN2B missense variants.
note: Citation position ambiguous.

content: Radiprodil's allosteric action is voltage-independent and not use-dependent, so it resembles d-APV in gating independence while adding GluN2B selectivity; hence closest mechanistic match.
note: Rests on class-level characterisation, uncited. Verifier X1: abstracts of the class prototypes say ifenprodil and Ro 25-6981 act in an activity-dependent manner (PMID 9003561, 9400004; read by the verifier only), so "not use-dependent" is contradicted for the class at abstract level and unverified for radiprodil.

content: In vivo, radiprodil dose-dependently rescued audiogenic seizures in GluN2A(N615S) gain-of-function mice; authors say it "may have the potential to control seizures in patients with GRIN2A GoF mutations".
note: Radiprodil rescued a GluN2A GoF model although it is a GluN2B-selective agent; report does not comment.

content: Radiprodil is the single agent that is both the closest mechanistic match and a direct test of the GluN2B hypothesis; a positive result validates translation and localizes burst to GluN2B.
note: Core recommendation. The "closest match to d-APV" rests on the uncited gating-independence premise (E14), which the class prototypes contradict at abstract level (verifier X1).

content: Ifenprodil and traxoprodil: GluN2B-selective allosteric modulators; tool comparators; matrix: tool/discontinued, good CNS exposure; lower priority.
note: Matrix scores "good CNS exposure" without citation.

content: Selfotel (CGS-19755) and perzinfotel: only agents sharing d-APV's competitive glutamate-site mechanism; abandoned for psychotomimetic/neurotoxic effects and excess mortality; not clinically used.
note: No citation for perzinfotel failure.

content: Selfotel phase-III trial was aborted for excess deaths and adverse events; described as "the competitive NMDA-receptor antagonist selfotel".
note: Basis for "competitive class void on safety grounds".

content: Whole spectrum of NMDAR antagonist classes failed neuroprotection trials: competitive (selfotel), channel blockers (aptiganel, dextrorphan), GluN2B/polyamine site (eliprodil), glycine site (gavestinel, licostinel).
note: Stroke/neuroprotection context, not epilepsy; transfer by shared-class logic.

content: Aptiganel, eliprodil, gavestinel, licostinel named in passing as failed neuroprotection agents (channel blocker, GluN2B/polyamine, glycine-site x2).
note: Compounds named in passing.

content: Competitive block (d-APV's own class) is the least translatable mechanism; allosteric/GluN2B agents are favoured.
anchor: L9,L41,L125 Summary; F005 title; Supported vs Refuted
note: Report scores matrix for developmental safety "+" for radiprodil while citing no developmental safety data for it (see E90).

content: Reviews conclude allosteric modulators have improved safety/therapeutic indices versus direct competitive or high-affinity channel-blocking antagonists; low-affinity channel blockers (ketamine, memantine) were the first-generation tolerated agents.
note: Review-level statement.

content: Survival-signaling rationale: "blockade of synaptic transmission mediated by NMDA receptors hinders neuronal survival" (Ikonomidou & Turski).
note: Used to argue NMDAR blockade harmful beyond acute effect.

content: In immature cortex GluN2B (NR2B) is the predominant GluN2 subunit: NR1/NR2B main extrasynaptic subunit with NR2B Y1336 phosphorylation in immature brain.
note: Species/region of the cited study not stated in the report.

content: In neonatal cortex NMDAR-mediated EPSCs are "largely mediated by GluN2B-containing NMDARs".
note: Species not stated.

content: WWOX burst is recorded in an immature GluN2B-dominant circuit, so a GluN2B-selective agent is developmentally matched and diagnostically informative; GluN2B identity of the burst is inferred from developmental expression, not measured in the WWOX preparation.
note: Report states the dominance argument is inferential at L128.

content: Which GluN2 subunit (GluN2A, GluN2B or mixture) carries the WWOX burst? Not measured.
note: Single most important datum.

content: Is the NMDAR drive underlying the burst tonic/sub-threshold (possibly extrasynaptic) or phasic/regenerative? Not characterized.
note: Dominates whether channel blockers can transfer.

content: If the burst depends on depolarized regenerative NMDAR current, channel blockers should suppress it efficiently, possibly more selectively than d-APV.
note: Branch of decision tree.

content: At physiological Mg2+ and resting potential a tonic NMDAR drive abolished by d-APV may be largely Mg2+-blocked and inaccessible to use-dependent blockers, so transfer to channel blockers would fail.
anchor: L11,L45,L76-L79,L157 Summary; F006; decision tree; Falsification
note: Internal logic: tonic current at rest is said to be Mg2+-blocked yet d-APV abolishing it implies it is NMDAR-mediated; no data.

content: Memantine and open-channel blockers are use-dependent, voltage-dependent and compete with physiological Mg2+ block; they reach only receptors open and unblocked, i.e. depolarized potentials during high activity Diagram L60 labels pore block "trapping".
anchor: L45,L60-L62,L67 F006; diagram; Why the transfer is not automatic
note: Matrix marks all pore blockers "Mg2+ site (-)", including ketamine, amantadine, N2O, DXM.

content: Voltage/Mg2+/use-dependence mismatch is the decisive experimental discriminator for whether channel blockers can reproduce d-APV.
note: Called "the decisive experiment".

content: A GluN2B NAM reaches only GluN2B-containing receptors; clinical success is contingent on driving subunit and tonic-vs-phasic character of the drive, which d-APV masks.
anchor: L67 Why the transfer is not automatic
note: Restates E03.

content: Decision tree: if burst is GluN2B-carried, radiprodil should reproduce d-APV; if not, radiprodil fails and the transfer to 2B agents is unjustified. If phasic, channel blockers (ketamine, memantine) should reproduce d-APV; if tonic, likely ineffective at physiological Mg2+ and a NAM is favoured.
note: Branches are not mutually exclusive with each other (two independent axes).

content: Developmental neuroapoptosis: WOREE seizures begin in first weeks to months, overlapping the human brain growth-spurt/synaptogenesis window; NMDAR blockade there "triggers neuronal suicide (apoptosis)".
note: Onset timing statement uncited.

content: NMDA receptor antagonists including ketamine "induce neurodegeneration in the developing brain".
note: Species not stated.

content: Agents acting at the channel Mg2+ site (MgSO4) cause caspase-3-positive developmental apoptosis, showing breadth of the liability.
note: Report treats MgSO4 as acting at a "channel Mg2+ site".

content: Ketamine channel block is enhanced and longer-lasting in immature versus mature cortical neurons: "a more extensive inhibition... in neonatal neurons than in adult neurons".
note: Used both for sensitivity-to-benefit and for harm; implies adult pharmacology cannot be extrapolated.

content: Developing cortex is simultaneously more sensitive to NMDAR blockade's benefit and its harm; even a pharmacologically successful transfer must clear a therapeutic-index bar (burst-suppressing concentration well below apoptotic concentration).
note: Same survival-signaling logic said to have sunk neuroprotection trials (E20, E24).

content: Therapeutic-index window (burst-suppressing vs apoptosis-inducing concentration) for these agents in the WWOX context is unmeasured.
note: none

content: Ketamine terminates refractory/super-refractory status epilepticus with pooled rate "56% (95% CI: 51-61)" across adults and children; mechanistically distinct, complementary to GABAergics.
note: Described as efficacy ceiling and feasibility.

content: Ketamine in neonatal status epilepticus appeared safe and effective, yet "Neurologic sequelae including hypotonia and spasticity were reported for 4/5 of the surviving children".
note: Small series; "safe and effective" and sequelae in same sentence.

content: ATP1A2-related DEE infant: seizure "partially responsive to ketamine, and she became seizure-free when memantine, another NMDA receptor blocker, was added".
note: Report calls it "the most direct precedent" and "direct monogenic-DEE precedent"; single case; combination with ketamine.

content: Neonatal nonketotic hyperglycinemia: ketamine and dextromethorphan reducing NMDA excitatory properties tried but "the outcome is usually poor".
note: Used to bound expectations with a partial-efficacy ceiling.

content: Feasibility is established in vivo: clinical NMDA antagonists already suppress NMDAR-driven seizures in neonates/infants.
note: Title says "NMDAR-driven seizures" though SE and ATP1A2/NKH are not shown NMDAR-driven.

content: WOREE is characterized by "early-onset drug-resistant seizures"; response of these syndromes to antiepileptic drugs is "very poor" and alternative approaches should be explored.

content: A mechanism-matched NMDA-antagonist route is rational (drug resistance) and novel (not yet explored in WOREE); to be framed as a complementary symptomatic hypothesis alongside, not displacing, gene-therapy and GSK-3beta arms.
